newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK stock market puts politics in back seat for now.
newsitem.headline: HK stock market puts politics in back seat for now.

text.p: Confidence in Hong Kong's smooth return to China has been a driving force for local shares, but politics has taken a back seat of late with a civil rights row failing to rile investors, analysts said on Monday.
"People are increasingly dismissive. Over the last year, Hong Kong has decided to turn a blind eye to politics," said Franklin Lam, director of research at HG Asia. "Everyone sees blue skies."
Generally smooth relations between Britain and China have had stock market punters calling for a removal of a political risk discount which has long dragged on the Hong Kong market.
The blue-chip Hang Seng Index hit an all-time high of 14,004.93 in mid-January, accompanied by a heavy flow of money into the Hong Kong market.
But a row broke out last week after a China-controlled committee unveiled plans to dilute laws on civil liberties in Hong Kong after Britain hands back the territory to China at midnight of June 30.
"This is a very bad signal," said Marshall Mays, chief strategist at Nikko Research Center (Hong Kong). "It looks very bad and it smells bad from an investors point of view."
"It could well be that it is just an issue of face. But if they start to go forward and visibly suppress debate, the place will shut down overnight," said Mays.
But with so much money at stake it may take a full international debate to push the issue to the fore, analysts said.
The near-term threat was more likely to be interest rates and the direction of the U.S. market, they said.
"The market is much more concerned about interest rates," said Howard Gorges, a director at South China Brokerage.
"I suppose you can't rule out some potential (impact) if it became international with America weighing in, but I suspect it is not going to reach that stage. It is still early days," he said.
Alan Hutcheson, director of research at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell, said China's move also came as no surprise.
"China always said that some of the reforms being made by the government were not acceptable," he said. "I think investors are still saying that they are confident about the handover."

Hong Kong's focus on big business was also an element of stability that investors were counting on, with shipping magnate Tung Chee-hwa at the helm as Chief Executive after the handover, analysts said.

"At the end of the day people just want to make money," said James Osborn, sales director at ING Barings. "Big business and property -- that is the driving force of the market. Politics is a sideshow which is very rarely important."
